summary: A fragment from a fiction novel (labeled Book 15, part 110) in which Ray Marlowe meets Amah, an older woman weaving a bark basket, in a room with Emma. Amah confronts Ray with sharp, blunt remarks about his manners, the family's troubles (Emma and Frederick's mother, Micah), and whether he can understand the Whiston family's situation. The exchange turns on truth versus perception and the meaning of courtesy, and the passage ends with Ray questioning the word 'courtesy.'
one_line: Ray Marlowe is scolded by the blunt, perceptive Amah over his manners and his ignorance of the Whiston family's troubles.
key_facts: Amah is weaving a broad, dun colored disk of plaited bark strips while she speaks to Ray Marlowe.
Amah tells Ray that he looks but does not gawk, which she says is better manners than he has shown toward the family so far.
Amah says Ray's mother had good handiwork that was blunted by less tactful teachers.
Ray apologizes reflexively, and Amah responds by listing his supposed faults, including manhandling Frederick after Frederick let his temper get the better of him.
Emma says in a small voice, 'Amah, this is Ray,' and Amah replies that she knows who he is.
Amah says the family has seen trial stacked on trial, citing Emma and Frederick's mother, then Micah.
Amah tells Ray that the affairs of the Whiston family are beyond his ken and asks whether he is a fool.
Emma draws a sharp breath and says, 'Amah, you promised.'
Amah states that the ability to separate truth from fiction is the foundation of courtesy.
Ray says that he has been apprised of the current situation, and Amah answers that he has no idea of its complexities.
The passage ends with Ray speaking the word 'Courtesy?'
